name: Bulin 47 AI Video Generator
tagline: Upload one photo, get a 12 second vertical clip of yourself doing the Bulin 47 street freestyle, sized for TikTok, Reels and Shorts.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. Sites in this genre normally sell credit packs per clip rather than seats.

verdictSummary: This is a preset wrapped around somebody else's image-to-video model, which is a fair description of most single-trend AI video sites. An agent can rebuild the whole loop in one sitting: file upload, a hardcoded prompt, a call to a hosted image-to-video endpoint, then ffmpeg to crop 9:16 and trim to 12 seconds. The part you cannot rebuild is the model, so you trade a credit pack here for an API bill there, and you will burn some of that bill discovering which prompt wording actually produces the dance instead of a person standing still. Call it buildable, not free. If you want one clip this week, buy the clip; if you want fifty variations and control over the preset, build it.
coreLoopDIY: A local web page that takes one photo, sends it to a hosted image-to-video API with a locked-in trend prompt, then crops and trims the result to a 12 second 1080x1920 MP4.
requirements: A fal.ai or Replicate account with credits and an API key
Patience and a small budget for prompt iteration, since each failed clip costs real money
Your own judgment about posting AI footage of a real person's face
whatYouLose: The tuned prompt. Theirs has presumably been iterated against hundreds of outputs; yours starts at guess one.
Prepaid GPU queue. Your clip waits behind whatever the provider's load looks like, with no fallback.
Maintenance of the trend. When the aesthetic mutates in three weeks, someone else updates their preset and nobody updates yours.
Phone-friendly flow. A localhost page is not something you use from the couch without extra plumbing.
Moderation and failure handling, so bad inputs just return an error blob instead of a polite retry.
moatNotes: The real asset is a prompt string plus whoever grabbed the trend keyword first. Neither survives the trend.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the demand is impulsive and the output is disposable. Nobody who wants a Bulin 47 clip wants to install ffmpeg, open a fal.ai dashboard and read model docs; they want the video before the trend dies. Paying a few dollars for a clip that works on the first try is rational when the alternative is an evening of prompt roulette at API prices. The build makes sense only if you are producing these at volume or want a preset nobody else controls.
notes: Single-trend video sites are a genre, not a product: the code is a weekend, the timing is everything.
prompt:
Build a local, single-user web tool that turns one uploaded photo into a 12 second vertical dance clip using a hosted image-to-video API. No accounts, no database, no telemetry, no cloud deploy.

Stack, non-negotiable: Next.js 15 with the App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind, and ffmpeg invoked as a child process. Node 22. Everything runs on localhost.

Flow:
1. One page at / with a drag-and-drop photo input (JPEG or PNG, max 10 MB), a textarea prefilled with an editable motion prompt, and a Generate button.
2. POST the image to a route handler at /api/generate. Save the upload to ./tmp with a uuid name.
3. The handler calls the fal.ai image-to-video endpoint using FAL_KEY from .env.local. Put the model id in a single MODEL_ID constant at the top of a lib/video.ts file so it can be swapped in one edit.
4. Poll the job, stream status strings back to the client with a simple Server-Sent Events response, and show them in a log pane. Do not fake progress bars.
5. When the provider returns a video URL, download it to ./out, then run ffmpeg to scale and center-crop to 1080x1920, trim to exactly 12 seconds, normalise to 30 fps, and write H.264 + AAC MP4.
6. Show the finished video in a player with a download link, plus the exact cost-relevant facts you know: model id, job id, duration.

Also build a /library page that lists every MP4 in ./out with its thumbnail (generate thumbnails with ffmpeg) and the prompt used, read from a sidecar JSON file per clip. Flat files only, no database.

Include in the repo: a .env.example with FAL_KEY, a README that states plainly that each generation costs money and that the prompt will need several attempts before the motion looks right, and a prompts.ts file holding three starter motion prompts as named presets.

Out of scope, do not build: user auth, payments, a job queue, social posting, watermark removal, face swapping of people who did not consent, or any hosted deployment config.
